nameStory: The tropical house gecko earned its name from its love of warm climates and its habit of moving into human homes uninvited! Unlike most of our native New England reptiles that hibernate through winter, this little lizard from sub-Saharan Africa seeks out the cozy warmth of heated buildings. It's also called the 'cosmopolitan house gecko' because it has hitchhiked around the world with human travelers, making itself at home on every continent.
description: The tropical house gecko is a small, pale lizard about 3-5 inches long with a chunky body and large eyes. Its skin has a translucent, almost ghostly appearance with a pinkish or grayish background marked by darker spots or bands. Unlike our native lizards, it has sticky toe pads that let it walk up walls and across ceilings with ease. This is definitely not a native New England species, but a few have been spotted as stowaways in shipments or escapes from the pet trade.

idTips.label: Toe Pads
idTips.description: Large, sticky toe pads on each finger and toe that feel slightly rubbery to the touch - no other New England reptile has these climbing adaptations

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Skin feels soft and slightly bumpy with tiny granular scales, very different from the smooth or keeled scales of native lizards

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent eyes with vertical pupils and no eyelids - they lick their eyes clean with their tongues

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Translucent pinkish-gray background with darker brown or gray bands across the body, often with a mottled appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active at night, often seen near lights hunting insects, and makes soft chirping or clicking sounds

habitat: In New England, tropical house geckos are only found indoors in heated buildings like greenhouses, pet stores, or homes where they've accidentally been introduced. They need consistently warm temperatures year-round and would not survive outdoors in our climate. Look for them near windows, light fixtures, or warm areas where insects gather.

seasonality.spring: May be slightly more active as building temperatures warm up, but indoor sightings remain rare and accidental.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time for new introductions through shipping or travel, though they remain inside heated buildings.
seasonality.fall: Activity may increase indoors as they seek warmest spots in buildings before heating systems start up.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - any sightings would be strictly indoors in heated spaces.

funFact: These geckos can literally walk on water! Their toe pads are so effective that they can run across the surface tension of a puddle without breaking through, making them one of the few vertebrates with this superpower.
confusionNotes: With only 3 sightings recorded in New England, confusion with other species is unlikely since we have no native geckos. The sticky toe pads and ability to climb smooth walls instantly separate it from any native lizard. Memory trick: 'Sticky toes = not from here!'
contextualKnowledge: This species represents an 'accidental introduction' - meaning it didn't arrive intentionally but as a stowaway in cargo or through the pet trade. While established populations exist in warmer parts of the U.S., New England's climate prevents them from surviving outdoors year-round.
compareHints: The tropical house gecko is larger and more robust than its relative the Mediterranean house gecko, with a chunkier build and more pronounced toe pads. Unlike the Indo-Pacific house gecko which reproduces without males, tropical house geckos require both sexes to breed. All three species share the same basic body plan of large eyes, sticky toes, and nocturnal habits that make them successful house guests worldwide.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mediterranean House Geckos are the most likely of the Hemidactylus genus to survive in New England's climate due to their cold tolerance and association with heated buildings.
Compared to its close cousin the Mediterranean House Gecko, the Indo-Pacific species has more pronounced spiny scales along the tail edges and tends to be slightly smaller overall.
